In my initial year there, I simply observed—shredding potatoes and dicing onions while others worked. By the following year, however, I'd taken charge: everything except the eggs went straight into the machine, and I announced I'd handle the latkes myself. I followed through, and my stack of golden, crackling results made its way to the table courtesy of my wife, a woman whose ways still puzzled me. In that apartment—which my in-laws insisted on calling a house, though pulsing new-wave beats came from one corner and marijuana smoke drifted from another—reading materials sat untouched, conversation dimmed, and cash held no value. There, she had bent down to recite, to an audience of none, the words a three-year-old had made into scripture: no more, no, no more, no.

The uncle whose fortune came from a single hit song piled three latkes onto his plate and dove in, launching into commentary about critics and Mayor Koch. By then everyone was crunching away, spreading on applesauce, sipping tea, while he moved on to Rabin, Mehitabel, broadcast radio, and Durrell, insisting that a genuine song must also function as poetry—and that the reverse held equally true. Finished, he aimed a grease-slicked finger at me and declared, loud enough for the whole room: "You can't possibly be a gentile. You're an honorary member of the tribe!" Against all odds, my latkes managed to earn that title for another five years running.

Then came the grief. Then came the emptiness that followed.

# The Latkes

It began humbly enough—standing at the edge of the kitchen, watching hands more practiced than mine grate potatoes into golden shreds, squeeze out the moisture, fold in the onion and egg. That first year, I was permitted only to peel and prep, to be useful in the way that outsiders are useful: present, but not essential. By the second year, something had shifted. I was trusted with the spatula, then the pan, then the whole operation—timing the oil just right, listening for that particular sizzle that meant it was ready to flip. Two years, and I had gone from spectator to the one standing over the stove while everyone else waited, plates in hand, for the first batch to cool enough to eat.

The gatherings themselves were a kind of beautiful chaos. Around the table, three generations argued and laughed in the same breath—my father-in-law holding forth on some political scandal from the morning news, his sister interrupting to recite a line of Neruda she'd memorized decades ago, a cousin's teenager defending a musician none of the older relatives had heard of. The conversation moved like water finding its level, seeping into every crack of silence, and somehow it all made sense together: policy and poetry, jazz and gossip, all of it seasoned with the smell of oil and potato drifting in from the kitchen.

In the middle of all this noise, I remember a smaller, quieter scene. My wife knelt on the floor beside our three-year-old, who had worked himself into that particular kind of toddler distress that defies logic. He kept repeating the same phrase—"no more no no more no"—not shouting it, but murmuring it, over and over, like an incantation. She didn't try to reason with him. She just stayed low, at his level, her hand on his back, letting the words wear themselves out like a wave losing its momentum against the shore. It was the kind of moment that happens in the margins of a big family gathering, easy to miss, but somehow it held its own kind of weight.

Later that evening, my wife's uncle—a man whose success in business was matched only by the seriousness with which he doled out approval—took a bite of the latkes and nodded slowly, the way he did when he was about to make a pronouncement. "Honorary Jew," he said, pointing his fork at me. It wasn't a title he gave lightly, and I understood, from the way the table went quiet for a beat before erupting into laughter, that I had passed some kind of test. For five more years, that title held. Every holiday, the latkes reaffirmed it—crisp at the edges, soft in the middle, proof that I belonged at that table.

And then—the wailing. And then—the dust.
outputs.L4:
The first year, I did nothing but watch.

I stood in the doorway of my mother-in-law's kitchen, a glass of wine sweating in my hand, while three women I barely knew argued in two languages about whether the potatoes should be grated by hand or by machine. My wife moved between them like water finding its level, laughing at jokes I only half caught, kissing cheeks, disappearing into the pantry for another sack of onions. I was new to all of it—the menorah in the window, the dreidels spinning across the coffee table, the smell of oil that would cling to the curtains for a week. I held my glass and nodded and felt, not unpleasantly, like a guest at someone else's history.

The second year, someone handed me a grater.

By the fourth, I had graduated to the food processor, and this, it turned out, was where I found my footing. There is a particular satisfaction in the mechanical shredding of potato and onion, the blade doing in seconds what once took an aunt's aching wrists an hour. I learned to squeeze the moisture out in a clean dish towel, to feel for the right dryness with my palms, to listen for the specific hiss of oil hot enough to crisp but not scorch. My latkes came out lace-edged and golden, holding their shape when flipped, shattering pleasingly at the first bite. I did not know yet that this small competence would become, for a time, a kind of identity.

The gatherings themselves had their own liturgy, separate from any prayer book. My wife's uncle, a man who had once played clarinet professionally and never let anyone forget it, brought his instrument every year and filled the living room with klezmer runs that made the children stamp their feet on the hardwood. Someone always read a poem—sometimes Yiddish, translated haltingly and with much interruption; sometimes something newer, written by a cousin who wanted desperately to be heard. There were debates about Israel, about assimilation, about whether Chanukah gelt was a capitalist plot, conducted with the particular ferocity that only people who love each other can sustain over a table of fried food.

Beneath all of it, my wife carried something she did not name. I noticed it most in the pauses—when she'd step out to the porch for air that wasn't cold enough to justify a coat, when her eyes would go distant during the candle-lighting, fixed on some middle distance none of us could see. I never asked directly. I learned the shape of her grief the way you learn the furniture in a dark room, by bumping into it gently, over and over, until you know where not to step.

And there was her sister's youngest, who for two years running refused to eat anything at all, who would sit at the corner of the table with her arms crossed and say, in a voice thin as paper, that she wasn't hungry, that she didn't want to be here, that she wanted to go home—though home was forty minutes away and she would return to it that same night. No one pushed. We had all, I think, wanted at some point to say the same thing.

It was the fifth year that the uncle—the clarinetist, the one everyone deferred to, whose approval functioned like a currency you didn't know you'd been saving—took a bite of my latkes and went quiet in a way that made the whole table pause. He chewed slowly, theatrically, the way he did everything. Then he pointed his fork at me and announced, to no one and everyone, that I was now an honorary Jew. The table laughed and someone clinked a glass and my wife's eyes were wet in the candlelight, though I couldn't have said if it was from that or from something older.

I carried that title for five more years. It became a joke that wasn't quite a joke, a line trotted out each December—here comes the honorary Jew, someone would say, watch him work the food processor. I liked it more than I let on. I liked belonging to something by way of grease and starch and a machine doing the labor my hands had never learned from a grandmother, because I had no grandmother in this story, only borrowed ones, only aunts who were not mine and a wife who had become the entire bridge.

Then came the wailing. Then came the dust.

I will not detail here the particulars of loss—whose death, which year, how the phone rang and how the room went sideways—only that the honorary title, like the uncle who bestowed it, like the potatoes that browned in oil each December, like the poems recited and the arguments won and lost, turned out to be exactly as durable as everything else we build against the dark. Which is to say: durable enough to matter, and not durable at all.

I still make the latkes. I still use the food processor, still squeeze the liquid from the shreds with a towel gone permanently onion-scented, still listen for the hiss that means the oil is ready. But I make them now the way you tend a grave—not because anyone requires it of me, but because the ritual is what remains when the reasons for it have gone quiet. The table is smaller. The clarinet sits in its case. Somewhere, perhaps, a child who once refused to eat has grown into someone who understands refusal differently.

The honor was fragile. I knew that even as I held it. But for those years, the potatoes crisped, the wine passed hand to hand, the poems were read aloud into a room full of people who loved each other loudly and imperfectly, and for those years, that was enough—was, in fact, everything, the way that only impermanent things can be.

# The Rabin-Karp Algorithm: Efficient String Matching Using Hashing

## Introduction

The Rabin-Karp algorithm, developed by Richard M. Karp and Michael O. Rabin in 1987, is a string-searching algorithm that uses hashing to find patterns within larger texts. It represents an elegant solution to a common problem in computer science: efficiently locating occurrences of a specific substring (the pattern) within a larger string (the text).

## How It Works

The core idea behind the Rabin-Karp algorithm is to avoid the computational expense of comparing every character of the pattern against every position in the text. Instead, it uses a hash function to compute a numerical representation of the pattern and compares this hash value against the hash values of substrings in the text of the same length.

The algorithm proceeds through these key steps:

1. **Compute the hash value** of the pattern
2. **Compute the hash value** of the first substring of the text with the same length as the pattern
3. **Compare the hash values** — if they match, verify character-by-character to confirm an actual match (avoiding false positives due to hash collisions)
4. **Slide the window** one position forward and use a rolling hash technique to efficiently compute the new hash value without recalculating from scratch
5. **Repeat** until the entire text has been scanned

## The Rolling Hash Technique

What makes Rabin-Karp particularly efficient is its use of a rolling hash function. Rather than recomputing the hash value for each new substring position from the ground up, the algorithm updates the previous hash value by removing the contribution of the outgoing character and adding the contribution of the incoming character. This operation can be performed in constant time, making the sliding process highly efficient.

## Time Complexity

In the average case, the Rabin-Karp algorithm achieves a time complexity of O(n + m), where n is the length of the text and m is the length of the pattern. However, in the worst case—when many hash collisions occur—the complexity can degrade to O(nm). Despite this potential worst-case scenario, the algorithm performs exceptionally well in practice, especially for applications involving multiple pattern searches.

## Practical Applications

The Rabin-Karp algorithm is particularly valuable in scenarios such as:

- **Plagiarism detection**, where multiple patterns need to be searched simultaneously
- **Digital forensics**, for identifying specific data signatures
- **Bioinformatics**, for searching DNA sequences
- **Network intrusion detection systems**, scanning for malicious patterns

## Conclusion

The Rabin-Karp algorithm remains a fundamental technique in computer science education and practical application. Its clever use of hashing to reduce unnecessary comparisons demonstrates how mathematical insight can transform a seemingly brute-force problem into an elegant and efficient solution. While other algorithms like Knuth-Morris-Pratt may offer better worst-case guarantees, Rabin-Karp's simplicity and effectiveness in multi-pattern searching ensure its continued relevance in modern computing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about making latkes with in-laws over several years, ending in loss and change.
counterfactuals.output:
# Latkes

The first year, your mother showed me
how to grate potatoes until my knuckles
nearly joined the pile of gold shreds,
laughing at my caution with the blade.
"Harder," she said, "you're not
apologizing to the potato."

We stood hip to hip at her counter,
the oil already ticking in the pan,
onions making us cry for reasons
we could pretend were only onions.

The second year I knew to squeeze
the liquid out with my bare hands,
knew where she kept the good salt,
knew the joke about your father
and the first latke, always sacrificed
to test the oil, always his to eat standing
at the stove like a toll he was owed.

Some years the kitchen was crowded—
your sister's kids underfoot,
someone's dog stealing scraps,
the window fogged with all our heat,
and your mother directing traffic
with a spatula like a conductor's baton.

Other years it was quieter.
Just the two of us and her,
the men watching football in the other room,
her hands slower now over the bowl,
mine finding the rhythm hers used to have,
the way you inherit a task
before you inherit the absence.

Last year she sat at the table
and told me what to do
without getting up.
I did not mind the changing of hands.
I did not know it was the last handing.

This year I stand alone at your stove,
the recipe unwritten because
it was never written,
only shown, only touched,
only passed like a secret
from palm to palm.

I grate too hard. I grate too soft.
I test the oil the way your father taught me—
sacrifice the first one, always,
though there's no one now to eat it standing up,

and still I make a plate for him,
still I make a plate for her,
because some griefs
you fry in oil and eat anyway,
because the potatoes don't know
who is missing from the table,

because some years
the latkes are perfect
and no one is here to see it,
and that, too, is part of the recipe now—
the burning, the missing,
the going on.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a narrative poem in first person about being an outsider at a Jewish family Hanukkah gathering, using specific sensory details like grated potatoes and applesauce.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Latke Table

I stand in Miriam's kitchen, hands empty,
not knowing where to put them or myself,
while her mother's arms move like she's conducted
this symphony a thousand times before—
the grater rasping against knuckles, potatoes
surrendering their pale flesh in ribbons,
onions weeping into the metal bowl
until my own eyes sting from three feet back.

"Sit, sit," she says, but I don't know this chair,
don't know if it belongs to some dead uncle
whose photo watches from the mantel, stern
in black and white among the brass menorah's
nine empty branches, waiting for the match.

The oil pops and hisses in the pan,
that sound of something transformative beginning,
and I recognize it from my own mother's kitchen—
grease finding its rhythm—though the words
they're speaking now dissolve before I catch them,
Hebrew or Yiddish, I can't tell the difference,
just music with consonants like small stones.

Miriam squeezes my hand under the table
where her grandmother won't see. "You're doing fine,"
she whispers, though I feel each glance that measures
whether I know the story, if I've heard
of oil that burned eight days instead of one,
if I know why we spin the dreidel, why
we count in gimmels, why the coins are chocolate.

The latkes come out amber, crisp as autumn
leaves before they crumble, and the applesauce—
her mother made it fresh, cinnamon and clove
still visible in flecks against the pale
gold puree, sweet enough to make my throat
ache with something like belonging, borrowed
for one evening, temporary as the candles
that will gutter out by morning, one by one.

I dip my fork in sour cream, then applesauce,
the way Miriam showed me, watching how
her father does the same, this small detail
a kind of citizenship I'm granted
for tonight. The children spin their dreidels,
laughing when they land on shin, on hey,
and I don't know the rules but clap regardless,
present in this room of candlelight and grease
and voices raised in blessing I can't speak
but recognize as prayer by how they bow
their heads, how something ancient moves through them
and touches me only at the edges,
warm as the oil, warm as this borrowed table
where I am welcomed, gently, as a guest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem that captures a multi-year memory of holiday cooking traditions, family banter, and a bittersweet ending marked by "wailing" and "dust."
counterfactuals.output:
**Flour on the Calendar**

Year one: Grandma's hands, dusted white,
kneading dough while uncles argued
whether cumin belonged in stuffing—
it didn't. She added it anyway.

Year two: the kids grew tall enough
to reach the counter without stools,
learned to roll pie crust like their mothers,
burned the first batch, laughed, tried again.

Year three: someone brought a turkey fryer,
nearly burned the porch down,
became the story told every year after,
embellished until the fire reached the sky.

Year four: new babies at the table,
old jokes recycled like foil,
Aunt Rita's cranberry sauce
still too tart, still devoured anyway.

Year five: the recipe cards grew stains,
coffee rings like tree rings counting time,
Grandpa's chair got quieter each year,
though we still set his plate from habit.

Year six: we didn't need the stools anymore.
The kids stood taller than the doorframe,
argued now like the uncles used to,
about cumin, about everything, about nothing.

Then the year the kitchen fell silent—
no clatter of pans, no debate over spice,
just wailing that filled the house
where laughter used to live,

and dust settling on the counters
where flour once rose like small ghosts,
on recipe cards no one dared to touch,
on chairs pushed in for good.

The oven door hangs open now,
cold, empty, holding nothing
but the memory of heat,
the echo of hands that shaped us

into something that still gathers,
still tries to season the silence,
still sets an extra plate from habit,
though no one comes to claim it.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary poem exploring themes of belonging and cultural identity through the ritual of frying latkes, referencing real names like Koch, Rabin, and Durrell.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Oil Remembers

My grandmother's hands knew the geometry of potatoes
before she knew the word *diaspora*—
the way a peeler surrenders skin in one continuous ribbon,
the way Koch's city once made room for her accent
between the deli counters and the subway grates,
Mayor Ed himself shaking hands at some Chanukah rally,
saying *how'm I doing* to a crowd that still remembered
which villages had disappeared, which names
had been sanded down at Ellis Island
like too much thumb against a grater.

She fries them in oil that spits like an old argument,
each latke a small continent
browning at its borders,
and I think of Rabin on that white house lawn,
the handshake that was supposed to mean
*we are done with exile, we are done
with drawing lines that bleed*—
how even peace looks like something fried too fast,
crisp outside, uncertain in the center.

I read Durrell once, his Alexandria
of mirrors and lovers and languages
folding into each other like batter,
and thought: this is what we do
in every diaspora kitchen—
we make a home from grated fragments,
we bind loose shreds with egg and matzah meal
because separation needs something
to hold it together, some starch
to keep the pieces from becoming only ash and oil.

My grandmother does not know Durrell.
She knows the sound a latke makes
when it's ready to turn,
that small sizzle-sigh, that exhale—
and maybe that's its own kind of literature,
maybe belonging was never about the treaty
or the mayor or the British novelist's sentence
curling like smoke above Egypt,
but about this: the spoon, the batter,
the particular gold of frying in December light,

the recipe passed down not in words
but in the httpwoowaork of hands over flame,
in knowing exactly when to flip,
when to let the second side
find its own particular brown,
the color of survival,
the color of a hundred kitchens
where the diaspora sits down to eat
and calls this, finally,
enough of a home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a personal, semi-autobiographical poem about being called an "honorary Jew" by an uncle during a family celebration, blending humor, nostalgia, and eventual sorrow.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Honorary Jew

Uncle Marty said it at Cousin Debra's bat mitzvah,
gin and tonic sweating in his hand,
clapping me on the shoulder like a rabbi
laying on some crooked blessing—
"You're an honorary Jew, kid,
you've earned it, all these years
eating my sister's brisket like you invented hunger."

I was twelve. I took it like a merit badge,
something to sew onto the sash
of an identity I didn't know I was stitching.
The women laughed. The men raised glasses.
Someone's grandmother pinched my cheek
and said *this one, he understands us*,
and I did not understand
that understanding isn't given,
it's carried, generation to generation,
like the good silver, like the scars.

I loved those Passovers—
the wine-stained Haggadahs,
the uncle who did all the voices,
Elijah's cup we filled and left,
the door cracked open to a hallway
that never held a prophet
but held instead the smell
of my aunt's kitchen, cinnamon and history,
and I was folded in,
a guest at a table set for grief and gladness both,
too young to taste the difference.

Now Marty's gone eleven years.
The bat mitzvah girl has children of her own
who call me something else, or nothing,
just *that friend of the family*
who shows up with the wrong wine
and stays too long at the door.

I think about the honor of it now—
how a joke can be a kind of grief rehearsal,
how "honorary" means
*we let you close enough to almost belong*
but the almost was the whole gift,
the whole terrible tenderness of it—
that I could sit at their table
and never once carry
what their table was built to remember.

I did not lose family in the fire.
I did not know the weight
of a name changed at Ellis Island
to something a mouth could swallow easier.
I only knew brisket, and laughter,
and an old man's hand on my shoulder
saying *you're one of us*
when neither of us
could say what that meant, exactly,
only that it was given freely,
only that it was, for one night,
enough to make a boy feel chosen
by something larger than his own thin history—

and now the boy is older
than Marty was that night,
and misses him
with a grief that has no ritual,
no prayer he's earned the right to say,
only the memory of a joke
that was, I understand now,
the closest thing to love
some men can hand you
across a folding table,
gin sweating, brisket cooling,
the whole broken beautiful family
still, somehow, singing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
